item.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
item.description: Royal Academy, London The modernist collector once ran a gallery in London – but from this confusing exhibition, it’s hard to tell what exactly was once in there Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky , Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy . item.description: An eight-hour docuseries looks back to explore the many problems and injustices that have helped to further break a broken system Lynn Novick’s new film for PBS is an epic, an eight-hour examination of Crime & Punishment in America . Beginning with justice in tribal societies, the documentary follows the arc of US history and ends in today’s troubled prison system, with the story of a podcast produced by prisoners in San Quentin and scenes from Rikers Island . “I’ve been working with Ken Burns on films about American history for all of my career, basically, and looked at the story of America through many different perspectives,” Novick said. “And honestly, I had never paid that much attention to the question of the justice system until 14 years ago, I had the opportunity to teach, to do a guest lecture in a college class inside a prison.” Continue reading...

item.title: A heretical outrage: why Italians disown spaghetti bolognese
item.description: Spag bol carries my city’s name all over the world – to the embarrassment of restaurants in Bologna In Bologna, spaghetti bolognese does not exist. You’ll find it on menus in London and Sydney, in British school canteens and in jars on supermarket shelves across half the world, but not in the city that lent it its name. Order it in a trattoria beneath the Two Towers and at best you get a pitying smile. More often you’ll be brought a plate of tagliatelle, with a short lesson in local history on the side. Few of the Italian dishes famous abroad carry the name of a city. Every so often the argument flares up again over where pizza, carbonara or tiramisu were born. With spaghetti bolognese the parentage is written into the name, and yet, absurdly, it is the Bolognese themselves who disown it. Many regard it as an outrage, a heretical and misshapen version cooked only by people who know nothing of real Bolognese food. Continue reading...

item.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
item.description: The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’ ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Continue reading...

item.title: Bows and old guns: Indigenous militias left to fight Peru’s cocaine gangs alone
item.description: Decades after Lima armed them to fight Shining Path rebels, the Asháninka are still defending their Amazon rainforest, but now against drug traffickers – and without any help Shielding his eyes from the tropical sun, Irmeo Sánchez Gómez – better known by his nom de guerre, Kiri – pointed up at a weathered shed on top of a hill, a few frayed sandbags piled at its base. Beyond it, the Tambo River snaked through Peru’s Amazonian rainforest. “When the terrorists came,” Kiri says, “they would shoot up at us from the riverbank. item.description: Blow to Kremlin as prestigious bridge linking occupied Ukrainian peninsula struck by missile. Plus, what is in store for Robert Pattinson, the new 007? Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Good morning. Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section. Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it. The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed that the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait. You can follow developments at the Apec and Asean summits with our live blog . Continue reading.

item.title: COP31: Corporate interests gain access to govt delegations participating in climate negotiations
item.description: Eve Irvine is pleased to welcome Siphesihle Mvundla, South African Climate and Energy Justice Campaigner at groundWork, a non-profit environmental justice organization. At COP31 in Turkey, representatives of major polluting industries have gained access to climate negotiations through government delegations, accredited organisations and other participation arrangements, according to research by the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition. Mvundla questions the extent of their involvement: "This year particularly, it's not just about the numbers, but it's about the influence that these private interests would have on the negotiations." While businesses have a role in implementing climate action, he questions their access to negotiations intended to regulate their industries and is calling for "an end to big polluter sponsorship and partnership at climate conferences" and insisted: "No more allowing big polluters to write the rules of climate action."

item.title: How the rightwing operative David Horowitz shaped Stephen Miller | Sidney Blumenthal
item.description: Horowitz, who swung from the far left to the far right, sought total political warfare against institutions and immigration Stephen Miller has risen to the top of the White House in the downdraft of Donald Trump’s abject defeat in the midterm elections. It is no irony to Trump that he has elevated Miller as his ideal bullying enforcer only after Trump’s own thorough repudiation. Appointing Miller is Trump’s denial that he is the worst thing he could possibly imagine: a loser. Trump has no more time for adults in the room who might want to negotiate with the new powers-that-be in the Congress. He has searched his soul, as he explained in his interview on 60 Minutes , entertaining his wish to ascend to heaven. Continue reading...

item.title: The NFL’s Salute to Service honors the military – and leaves out the realities of war | Lee Escobedo
item.description: This month, the league rightly honors veterans across the US. But little is mentioned about the death tolls, or the reasons behind our wars My mom taught me to thank veterans. Whenever we saw someone in a veterans hat, she set the example. Nobody in her family served, but my paternal grandfather fought in the Pacific in the second world war, and she was always grateful to hear his stories, even the repeats. It’s one of the things she gave me that I held on to, even in my worst years. The anger I’ve carried about the unjust wars of my lifetime – Afghanistan, Iraq and now Iran – never targeted the people sent to fight them. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
item.description: Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds. Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic . “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “I

item.title: I got scammed on Instagram – and it led to a truly disgusting dinner | Zoe Williams
item.description: Intrigued by an unusual recipe for spinach tacos, I followed the instructions, but was left with a soggy, inedible mess. It turns out there are a lot of made-up meals out there I can’t tell you when my Instagram algorithm changed, from – this is embarrassing, but what the hell – buff guys trying to exercise and being interrupted by a Staffordshire bull terrier who wants to help them exercise, to cooking videos, but it has. I now get endless food content, following the same format: a millennial has 20 minutes to make dinner for his or her beloved (it’s very gender neutral), and launches into some unlikely techniques. He might shove a load of chicken into a cake tin, sprinkle mismatched spices all over, bake it, then slice it, as if it were a cake. Or she might cook tagliatelle in a pan of milk and salmon. This is not how it’s done, I think, as I watch all the way to the end, and then am astonished to be fed yet more weird food content. Drawn with an almost zombified lack of free will, I

item.title: American Doctor review – medics put their lives on the line in Gaza amid the carnage
item.description: Poh Si Teng’s powerful documentary follows three doctors from the US who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital This is the latest documentary about medics travelling to Palestine to treat civilian casualties; it’s a powerful, angry film, in a state of despair at the scale of suffering and devastation. A sliver of hope is the trio of doctors it profiles, individuals acting on their conscience. (The same can be said of director Poh Si Teng , who quit her job at ABC News and cashed in her savings to get the documentary off the ground.) It follows three American doctors who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025 – though one of the trio, Thaer Ahmad, an ER doctor of Palestinian heritage from Chicago, is refused entry the night before they enter Gaza. His colleagues, Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon, and Dr Mark Perlmutter, a Jewish-American orthopaedic surgeon, complete the mission. This is not the first time in Gaza for either of them. It was 2014 and Hrdy was conducting an experiment. Having recorded a 63% jump in oxytocin in her saliva after spending hours cuddling the baby, she wanted to find out if something similar would happen to his hormones. It did, although it took a day longer. item.description: As Sylvester Stallone’s Oscar-winning drama celebrates its 50th anniversary, I Play Rocky helps to further turn the boxing hero into the stuff of legend The story behind the making of Rocky has always sounded uncannily like Rocky itself. An unknown with an improbable dream, a skeptical establishment and a refusal to accept the odds: Sylvester Stallone’s real-life struggle to crack the industry and bring his breakthrough film to the screen contained all the elements of the underdog story he sought to tell. Now, half a century later, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky has crafted those parallels into a crowd-pleasing yarn of its own. It’s an extraordinary afterlife for a modest boxing flick that became the highest-grossing film of 1976 on a $1m budget and won the Oscar for best picture over one of the most stacked fields in history. item.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
item.description: The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele. item.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
item.description: Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought . Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come. Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable. Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm Continue reading...

item.title: Automated warfare is already here. Now governments must restrain it | Helen Clark
item.description: AI systems can allow militaries to find and annihilate targets within seconds. A meaningful treaty must prioritise human control – and accountability Helen Clark is former head of the UN Development Programme and former prime minister of New Zealand, and member of The Elders Militaries around the world are increasingly relying on artificial intelligence to find, track and annihilate targets. An upcoming conference in Geneva offers a chance to confront the gravest risks of AI-enabled warfare, ideally through a treaty to regulate autonomous weapons systems. item.title: Heysel 85 review – rage-filled denunciation of the incompetence that fuelled a football disaster
item.description: Teodora Ana Mihai and her passionately committed cast reconstruct the grim sequence of bad judgments that led to 39 fans dying Shame and rage are the keynotes of this immersive, viscerally powerful drama-thriller set amid the macabre tragedy of football’s 1985 European Cup final between Juventus and Liverpool in the crumbling Heysel stadium in Brussels. Crowd disorder before kickoff in a poorly maintained, badly policed venue resulted in the deaths of 39 fans. In this film, the roar of the crowd echoing overhead through the stadium’s claustrophobic tunnels is like the wailing of the damned, while the sport’s officer class flinch and panic as if at a wartime loss. Grimly, the match was allowed to go ahead, despite the fatalities; the authorities believed the game itself would restore order on a bread-and-circuses basis, and that abandoning the match would only cause greater violence and chaos. Heysel 85 is directed and co-written by Romanian-born and Belgian-based film-maker Teodora Ana

item.description: Fifteen years on, this expansive follow-up to the campus epic explores female agency, friendship – and the messiness of early adulthood Back in 2011, Chad Harbach’s debut The Art of Fielding was hailed as the next Great American Novel. Set on the campus of Westish, a fictional midwestern liberal arts college, and steeped in baseball, it grappled with the big, quintessentially American themes – ambition, failure, the pursuit of perfection – that have traditionally been the genre’s hallmark. Harbach himself winkingly invited the categorisation: The Art of Fielding communes directly with the spirit of Herman Melville, arguably the greatest Great American Novelist of them all. Westish College, the novel explains, has claimed Melville as its own since the discovery of a lecture he gave there in 1880: its baseball team is known as the Harpooners; and a Melville statue presides over the campus like the genius of the place. When I turned up in shorts to interview the actor, he lent me his jacket, but I suspect he may have regretted it The biting flies were wild in Toronto in September 2012. A colleague and I were there to cover the film festival, but our key reference that year was a zinger from the 2007 cartoon Bee Movie, when it turns out Chris Rock’s mosquito has become a lawyer: “I was already a bloodsucking parasite,” he says, “all I needed was a briefcase!” (Bee Movie is one of the most brilliant and adult children’s movies ever; its central premise compares the honey industry to concentration camps.) Anyway, I spent the first week getting ever more bloodless and lumpy. We even shot a video about them, spraying repellent in front of us like Mace. It didn’t work. Every morning I woke bumpier than before. Continue reading...

item.title: The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings
item.description: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Here’s what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid Do you peel your potatoes, deseed your squash and core your cauliflower? A study by King’s College London , published last month in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition , found that people who routinely discard peels, skins, stalks and seeds when preparing fruit and vegetables are missing out on a valuable source of dietary fibre. Ten out of the 12 types of produce the researchers analysed had higher levels of fibre in the scraps than in the flesh. Eating these often overlooked parts could help address the global dietary fibre deficit and tackle food waste, they say. Here, experts share their advice on how to cook and eat “root to tip”. item.description: He is the maestro of American melancholy. But in a new biography, the artist is called a ‘sadist’ and a ‘prize hog’ by his wife – who was aghast to see their domestic and bedroom problems surface in his most famous works It should have been a happy occasion. In 1950, an Edward Hopper retrospective was staged at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York – but the artist’s wife, the painter Josephine (Jo) Nivison Hopper, was in a fury. The show’s catalogue, written by the museum’s director, had originally stated that in 1924 Edward “married the artist Josephine Nivison Hopper”, yet in the final version, the phrase “the artist” had been removed. “I’m not allowed to exist even in my husband’s biography,” Jo seethed in a private notebook that has just come to light. “And that’s all right with EH.” Due to her own strenuous efforts, Jo not only exists, but is a vital protagonist in my new biography of Edward Hopper. item.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
item.description: It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing? In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate . In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble. You just wish for even more interrogation – and for a therapist to step in Like film-maker and journalist Poppy Jay’s previous (excellent) documentary, Young, British and Anti-Abortion , her latest offering should come with a warning and blood pressure medication for all women watching. Some men, too, I’m sure, but you’ll forgive me if I can’t quantify the proportion. In Young, British and Tradwife, Jay interviews three women in the UK who are advocating the lifestyle that first took off as a social media phenomenon in the US (where the evangelical Christianity and social conservatism with which it is enmeshed are stronger influences than here). Each of the trio has been chosen with care and balance to represent slightly different manifestations of the movement. Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
item.description: From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “ war minus the shooting ”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday? My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. Described as a master of the pan-African novel and a literary giant, the 98-year-old received obituaries internationally, and in both French- and English-language African media. Le Monde called him “iconic”. item.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
item.description: Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989. Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. item.title: Not All Those Who Wander Are Lost album review – Anna Lapwood journeys to middle earth

Remarkably, she transcribed all but one segment by ear, a feat in itself. That she manages to tell the story chronologically over a 38-minute, three-movement span is equally impressive. But wait, there’s more. Reckoning the symphony would benefit from the human voice, she incorporated a handful of songs, performing them live – in Tolkien’s Elvish dialect – while playing the Nidaros Cathedral organ in Trondheim, Norway. The results are frequently convincing, though the folksy music of the Shire is less effective on the organ than the baleful music of Sauron and the Ringwraiths. item.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
item.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

item.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained

Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

item.description: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

The findings challenge fears that exercise worsens injured knees and could transform how patients recover from ACL reconstruction.

item.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
item.description: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. The findings support a century-old theory that royal attendants were sacrificed when kings died, possibly to serve them in the afterlife.

Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations. After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weathe

item.title: Sheherazaad: Khudgarzi review | Ammar Kalia's global album of the month
item.description: (Erased Tapes) Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr , in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. While her contemporaries such as the singers Ganavya and Manizeh draw on spiritual vocal traditions, and Arooj Aftab on jazz and folk instrumentation, Sheherazaad’s work is darker and far more introspective, using sparse acoustic arrangements to create a style of Urdu-language noir. On this debut album, she delivers her most disarmingly eerie and mournful work yet. A heavy layer of reverb coats the record’s spare and often evocative arrangements, making undulating tabla hits echo beneath Sheherazaad’s keening vocals on Qatil, while on Registaan it lends an unnervingly distorted quality to a simple guitar refrain and on Mard it subsumes melody in a ha

item.title: Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

item.title: A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
item.description: Stanford researchers have discovered that children who struggle persistently with math may have underlying differences in how their brains manage problem-solving strategies. item.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
item.description: Order a Diet Coke or invade Iran – that’s the choice facing the US president in one of several satirical games, as designers turn the gamification of politics back on the White House In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. item.title: Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson
item.description: Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013 For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking , consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one. The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining. Continue reading...

item.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
item.description: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

item.title: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising way that fructose, a sugar commonly found in sweetened foods and drinks, may help aggressive ovarian cancer spread. item.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. item.title: Bone broth, sweets ban and acupuncture: Harry Kane’s road to record England cap
item.description: Obsessive attention to detail is helping striker to reach new heights – and a 126th international appearance on Thursday It was Harry Kane’s dirty little secret. Something the England captain got up to after matches. He felt he deserved the indulgence. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September. No more. At the beginning of last season, Kane took the decision to cut out the naughty treats. After a while, he noticed a difference. He felt sharper; able to sprint more, make a greater number of accelerations. Was it down to this latest entry on the list of personal sacrifices? Or was it a consequence of his broader health regime, the scope of which is mind-blowing? Continue reading...

Measurements in living cells, together with molecular-dynamics simulations, show that flexible protein chains that form the selectivity barriers of nuclear pores are highly mobile, and that a sugar modification and the carrier protein importin-β help to preserve this dynamic state.

item.title: How to avoid aliens and live
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03515-z Silence is golden.

item.title: Earth’s early history told by 3.9-billion-year-old rocks from northern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03499-w Ancient rocks in northern China reveal that by 3.95 billion years ago, surface-altered oceanic crust had been buried rapidly to depths greater than 50 kilometres and partly melted. This crust was derived from a mantle reservoir that had been left behind when the crust separated from the early mantle as early as 4.3 billion years ago.

item.title: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03621-y Agricultural biotechnology once found itself in opposition to environmental science. Now it could reduce the impact of food systems on global warming and biodiversity loss.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03183-z Cliff Kapono shares his advice on ways to navigate and grow two different careers.

item.title: Hideki Shirakawa obituary: chemist who showed that plastics can conduct electricity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03633-8 Nobel prizewinner’s accidental discovery led to new forms of materials, light-emitting diodes and solar cells.

item.title: Give biologists the space to be curious, not just better tools
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03669-w Technology is making biological studies more powerful than ever. But people are the real force behind discovery.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5 A fresh approach considers waist circumference, rather than just weight and height, providing a more accurate classification.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2 The brain relies on crucial proteins to maintain neurons. This system is disrupted in mice with neurological disease.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03412-5 Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is leading a community of interdisciplinary specialists exploring how to make the energy use of artificial intelligence net-positive.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03624-9 Decades-old papers are increasingly being pulled from the literature, bringing a host of challenges.

item.title: Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7 An analysis of who is more likely to get authorship than acknowledgement highlights the influence of a researcher’s gender and status.

item.title: Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03641-8 Scientists are editing microbes to supply more nitrogen to staple crops.

item.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03425-0 A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

item.title: Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03274-x Once the promotion prospects of bureaucrats became tied to birth targets, the country’s one-child policy became more effective. Can the state now reverse this effect?

item.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03409-0 As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

item.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

item.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11232-w Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

item.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

item.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

item.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

item.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7 IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

item.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

item.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11259-z The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

item.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

item.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11280-2 Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

item.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

item.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11240-w A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

item.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2 Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
